This report documents the planned outage that has been completed on a SAC type steam 
turbine unit with the serial number 155360. 
The scope includes major inspection of both steam turbine and generator for Dead Sea 
Works Unit 3, which is operated as a backup unit for the last few years. This outage is a 
transactional maintenance works. Fieldcore team planned and executed the outage with craft 
labor provided by Fieldcore or by its subcontractor. 
There was one EHS specialist supplied by Fieldcore both at day and night shift. The NDT 
inspections of the unit were performed by a subcontractor. The outage was started on 22 
November 2019.
Prior to outage start, it was planned to replace all the old parts with new the parts when 
possible. This was agreed with the customer during the start of the outage.
 Therefore, the main parts given below has been changed with the new ones;

The other parts change depended on the condition and availability of the part.

Part Description: 
The turbine rotor disassembled and put on the rotor stands that customer has provided. A 
visual inspection has been carried out and ER case ER-20191204-0537 opened for findings. 
The critical findings were the indication seen on a blade near the notch at stage 14, heavy 
rubbing and material build up on the blade covers at the first 6 stages. To be sure of the 
indication an stage 14 blade, red dye inspection done on the indication and confirmed that 
the indication was a crack. 
During this time, transportation skid was modified per the turbine rotor dimensions. After 
that, the DSW Rotor (SN# X1352333) was shipped to the NIDCO facility for blast clean and 
NDT. All blasting occurred outside of the NIDCO facility and while the rotor was still in the 
shipping stands. It should be noted that this made it difficult to perform a thorough A/O 
cleaning, as did the turbine competency of the cleaners.  
After the rotor was A/O blast cleaned, magnetic particle inspection was performed on the 
rotor surface. A crack at the 14th stage special blade (next to the notch) was observed. This 
crack was also visually found during disassembly of the rotor. During further inspection, 
some surface indications on the 14th stage wheel were found where the notch is cut into the 
wheel. The indications were lightly polished and removed as it was determined to be a fab 
line from making the wheel notch or installing the blades.  
The 14th stage blade indication was evaluated by Engineering under ER Case 
ER-20191211-0177. The final resolution implemented was to cut the blade just under the 
area of indication. GE OSS was mobilized to the NIDCO facility to execute this work. The 
blade and cover were removed with caution to remove minimal material and to save all 
material removed. The material removed was weighed after removal and totaled 263.5 
grams. NDT was conducted after the blade was lightly profiled to remove any sharp edges or 
upset material. No indications were found. 
Built up metal material was noted in several areas of the rotor. This material was from spill 
strip damaged caused by a reported loss of oil and bearing wiping event. The amount of 
material ranged from stage to stage. The most severe areas were the 2nd and 6th stage that 
are shown in the accompanied pictures. The metal build-up was hand dressed by GE OSS 
while still onsite.  
Rotor Low Speed Balancing (LSB) commenced on approximately January 5th, 2020. IMHP 
provided the LSB skid to the NIDCO facility. A subcontractor was utilized to record and 
analyze the unbalance data. A separate GE OSS bucket/balance technician was mobilized 
to site for direction and staking of the balance weights. The LSB process proved difficult for

Part Condition: Good
Part Description: 
The nozzle box was removed from the casing together with the turbine rotor. Special tooling 
(bearing assembly) was used to position the nozzle box on the rotor. After removal of the 
stub shaft (coupling) and rotor gear ring, the nozzle box was rigged and removed from the 
rotor.
The nozzle box was sent to NIDCO workshop for cleaning and inspection. Aluminum oxide 
blast cleaning was performed on all critical area, followed by visual and NDT inspections.
Visual inspection revealed a good condition of the whole nozzle box assembly, except the 
spill strip that was found damaged at the lower/bottom side. Decision was made to remove 
the upset material and reuse the spill strip as is. Replacement of the spill strip would be time 
consuming and requires new parts and machining preparation. It may be scheduled for 
replacement during a future major outage.
NDT inspection revealed a good condition of the nozzle box assembly as well, except an 
indication found on the weld of the upper access plug. The indication was removed by light 
grinding/blending and. the area was NDT retested.
The valve seat sealing rings were found stuck and could not be moved due to the oxide 
deposits. Decision was made to replace the seal ring assemblies with new parts. The old 
parts were removed, the seal ring bores were cleaned, and the new ring assemblies were 
measured, fitted and locked per specification. Extensive cleaning was performed inside the 
nozzle box prior and after sealing rings installation.
The nozzle box was installed first in the casing for alignment purpose. The lower half packing 
housing was installed and dowelled in place, and the nozzle box was installed in the casing 
on the original shims for the alignment readings.
Finally, the nozzle box was installed on the rotor then inside the casing together with the 
rotor. The original support shims were reused, no additional machining was required as the 
alignment was found within acceptable limits.  New bolting hardware was installed at both 
horizontal joint and vertical joint with proper gap and/or torque tightening. All bolting was 
locked per design. New N1G6 packing ring was installed, however the original packing ring 
was installed at N1G5 location due to the lack of spare new part.
Before V1 vale installation, the nozzle box sealing rings were lubricated and aligned by using 
a special alignment tool fabricated at customer’s machine shop.

Part Description: 
After removal from the casings, all diaphragms were sent to NIDCO workshop for cleaning 
and inspection. Aluminum oxide blast cleaning was performed on all critical area, followed by 
visual and NDT inspections.
Most of the diaphragm nozzle/partitions were found in good condition and appropriate for 
further service. Several exceptions were noted and are documented below:
Light to medium partition damage was noticed on Stage #3 and Stage #4 diaphragm 
partitions. The noticed damages consisted of pipping like indications, and bending of the 
partition trailing edges, possibly FOD. Repair options were discussed with GE Engineering, 
documented by ER-20200107-0461. The final decision was made to cut back the trailing 
edges up to 1/8” and reprofile the partition in order to correct the partition surface and to 
restore the trailing edges thickness per drawing. All these repairs were performed by GE 
certified diaphragm technicians. NDT (LP) was performed on all partitions after repair and no 
indication was reported.
An indication was detected on one partition of Stage #11 U/H diaphragm. The indication was 
removed by grinding and the partition was restored by welding and hand machining. The 
repair was performed by GE certified diaphragm technician. NDT (LP) was performed after 
repair and no indication was present.
Two partitions were found damaged/bent, one on each Stage #17 Upper half Diaphragm and 
Lower half diaphragm respectively, both located at the HJ area. It is assumed that the 
damages occurred during transportation and handling. Both partitions were straightened, 
weld repaired and restored by GE certified technicians. NDT (LP) was performed after 
repairs and no indication was reported.
Inspection of the other diaphragm components (diaphragm webs, rings, horizontal joints, 
keys, dowels, support lag assemblies, set screws etc.) did not reveal major issues, except 
the conditions documented below:
An indication was reported following NDT inspection of the Stage #3 diaphragm, located on 
the diaphragm web, exit side, running from the packing drain hole down to the partitions. 
Further investigation revealed that the reported indication was a light erosion trace. It was 
removed by light polishing and NDT (LP) re-tested. Finally, the component was released for 
service.
Significant damage was found at all diaphragm spill strips, bottom side. The damage was 
most probably related to the loss of bearing supply oil and bearing failure event experienced 
in 2011. At that time the bearing babbitt was partially wiped out due to the shaft rotation

Part Condition: Good
Part Description: 
The Trip Throttle Valve (TTV) was removed and shipped to NIDCO for disassembly, cleaning, 
inspection, any repairs, parts replacement, and reassembly during this outage. Prior to GE/
FieldCore arrival to the NIDCO shop, the valve upper head “bonnet” was removed and the 
Pressure Seal Head (PSH) pull down ring disassembled. It was reported that the upper head 
nuts were not easily disassembled. The use of hydraulic wrenches in combination with 
heating the nuts with a torch was needed to remove the nuts. One (1) stud was cut during 
disassembly, which was not advised by GE/FieldCore. 
After the TTV upper head was removed, the TTV casing was stood upright and the TTV 
assembly removed. The TTV assembly looked to generally be in good condition. No steam 
erosion, visual cracks, or signs of stressing or overheating were visually observed.  A small 
gall in the TTV casing at the PSH fit was noted but looked to be old damage. Dimensional 
checks were conducted on the old TTV assembly to have some type of baseline as the 
dimensional data is not available from the Gimpel OEM manufacturer. All dimensional 
inspections can be found on the accompanied data sheets. 
The TTV casing was Aluminum Oxide grit blast cleaned during this outage. The flanges 
welds, valve seat welds, anti-swirl dam, and gasketed surfaces were all blast cleaned then 
dye penetrant tested (PT). Porosity was found on the small flange welds in several 
areas. One (1) small indication was also found on a leak-off flange. It was determined that 
the indication was undercutting from the toe of the weld pass above it. The steam dam had 
several areas of porosity noted. The valve seat was PT tested with no indications 
reported. The upper head studs were cleaned and Ultrasonically Tested (UT). No indications 
were noted. 
The TTV assembly was assembled with all new parts with the exception of the main disc 
valve cap. A new valve stem, PSH, PSH backseat, split rings, pilot valve, pilot valve cap, and 
valve cap pin were used. The pilot valve cap and main disc valve cap bolts only came with 
one (1) bolt each. The most damaged bolt on each cap was removed from service and 
replaced new. For All critical dimensions were rechecked and recorded on the accompanied 
data sheets.  There were some areas that were found to be different between the two (2) 
assemblies, but nothing that appeared to be compromising to the operation of the valve. The 
pilot valve was assembled with a new gasket during reassembly. There was a small gap 
under the cap after the bolting was final torqued, but it is unknown if that is by design. The 
pilot lift check was notably different from the assembly removed from service and the new 
assembly.

was not reassembled at the NIDCO facility. 
TTV Studs:
One (1) TTV stud was cut during disassembly of the upper head. Another stud was found 
backed out and determined to need removal, as the stud engagement was less than one 
times the diameter of the stud. To prevent damage to the bolt hole, the stud was cut off at the 
joint and drilled out with the other stud that was cut. Both bolt holes were tapped by a tap 
supplied by NIDCO after the stud shanks were removed. New studs were not available while 
the valve was at NIDCO so therefore not installed at the shop.
Two (2) small studs (Part 108 on TTV OEM Drawing NP-2312) were broken during 
disassembly. These studs are the studs that are on top of the upper head. It’s unclear to the 
writer why the flange was removed at all. The studs were drilled out of the upper head by 
NIDCO. New studs were made from bolting that was cut from the TTV upper head studs. The 
original studs were then misplaced and two (2) more studs made from an old casing 
bolt. The studs were installed after the valve was shipped back to site. 
TTV Steam Strainer:
The TTV steam strainer was blast cleaned and NDT’d during this outage. The strainer looked 
to be in good condition. A few of the screen holes were found to be oversized from 
presumably a previous repair or removal of debris. The holes were left as-is during this 
outage but are recommended to be planned for plugging during the next outage. 
During the TTV steam strainer NDT small indications were found at the welds securing the 
strainer to the upper head. There were a total of eleven (11) indications. The indications were 
ground by NIDCO under the direction of FieldCore. Previous Engineering Case 
ER-20160217-1896 was used as a guide during the repair, as this valve was provided by 
Gimpel under the same GE specification drawing. The rod selected in the case (E16-8-2) 
was not readily available in Israel. For this reason, a substitute Inconel rod was used per 
other similar PAC case. All welds were NDT’d after welding complete with no indications 
noted.

Hydraulic actuator cylinder’s inner surface and piston (guide side skirt surface) were noted 
with slight score marks, cleaned with finest oiled emery cloth and ScotchBrite.
Relay valve was disassembled from actuator cylinder, cleaned and fitted with new o- rings.

- Relay piston ring
- Spindle roller bearing
- Round paper gaskets (2x) for gear housing and square Garlock gasket for relay valve

Little information is available on the Gimpel valves. It is recommended that the OEM be 
consulted prior to the next outage for critical dimensional data if the valve assembly is to be 
reused and to have a baseline for new parts as it is the writer’s opinion that new parts should 
also be inspected as a quality best practice.  
The TTV steam strainer was found with a few perforations (holes) that were oversized at 
some point. GE DWG# 165A974BE specifies that these perforations be no larger than 
3/16”. It is recommended that prior to the next outage the GE team submit an ER case to 
engineering with direction on how to repair the holes. The specification outlines that the 
strainer should be made of 300 series SS, preferably 304 or 316. The site team should 
inquire to engineering for recommendations if the screen can be directly welded or pins 
should be fabricated and sized to each enlarged hole specifically. The GE team should also 
inquire what welding rod can be used that would be compatible for all 300 series stainless 
steel. 
Valve piston score marks are recommended to be monitored. Before next steam turbine’s 
inspection, a visual inspection is suggested through cover disassembly and relay valve 
removal to provide borescope access.

Part Description: 
V1 Valve Gear:
The V1 valve gear was disassembled, cleaned, inspected, repaired, parts exchanged, and 
reassembled at the NIDCO facility during this outage. After the valve was disassembled the 
steam chest was aluminum oxide blast cleaned and NDT’d. The results of the NDT section 
are discussed in the “Steam Chest” section below. All areas of the V1 valve gear assembly 
were inspected and can be summarized in their respective sections below. The most severe 
finding were the bushing and seat bores. It is recommended next outage to re-bore these 
areas and install oversized seats and bushings.
After the new parts were installed, cleaned, measured, etc., the V1 valve gear was 
reassembled at the NIDCO facility. All parts that were provided from the customer stock 
order prior to the outage were used. Two (2) of the new valve bushings per PN# 
101C459CA-1 that were allocated to the #3 and #4 V1 CVs were found with insufficient 
internal diameters. The stems could not be freely inserted into the bushings. Other than this 
issue no major issues were encountered when reassembling the V1 control valve.   
Steam Chest:
The V1 control valve steam chest was NDT’d after completion of the A/O blast cleaning. Two 
(2) indications were found during the inspection. One (1) small indication was found at the #3 
valve seat flange location. The indication was found at the gasket sealing area. ER Case 
20191226-0131 was generated for engineering disposition. The indication was left as-is. This 
is largely due to the location of the indication. It is recommended to monitor the indication 
during the next outage inspection. 
The second indication was found internal to the steam chest. This indication has likely been 
in the casing for several years of operation. The crack does exceed the criteria for no action 
outlined in EM 2502. However, due to the location of the crack it was left as is. Both 
indications should be monitored next outage. If the indications propagate, they should be 
removed, and engineering consulted to evaluate if the indications need repaired after 
excavation. 
The V1 control valve steam chest was thoroughly cleaned prior to reassembly. All flange 
surfaces were cleaned and stoned. All bolt/nut spot faces were cleaned and polished to 
remove any upset metal from previous bolting cycles.

surfaces corresponding to the DU bearing locations were PT tested. No indications were 
found. The shaft was also UT inspected. During the UT inspection an indication was found 
(measuring from either end) near the pinion gear. No action was taken this outage. A spare

on GE DWG 128C129BF , Zone C-5. All final camshaft bearing block IDs are provided on

The V1 valve springs were cleaned and inspected during this outage. After cleaning and a 
visual inspection, the springs were magnetic particle inspected. No indications were 
found. The valve spring free lengths were then measured and can be found on the 
accompanying data sheets. The #3 valve spring was found under the design minimum length

Stem dimensions and runout checks were conducted on the new stems, as well as bore 
dimensional checks on the new bushings. No issues were found during the checks. However, 
issues were encountered during assembly of the new bushings designated for the #3 and #4 
CV locations. The stems would not freely insert into the valve bushings. Several attempts 
were made to find a burr/high spot, loosening the bushing, and even light honing. The 
bushings were eventually removed and machined by NIDCO to be in acceptable 
conditions. NCR-20200107-0232 was generated to capture the issue.

Stem Bushing and Seat Bores:
Prior to installing the stem bushings and seats, the ID of the bores in the steam chest were 
measured. In both areas, on all valves, the holes were worn elliptical and oversized. The 
stem bushing fits ranged from 0.002” to 0.009” (100% to 400%) oversized. The seat fits 
ranged from 0.013” to .041” (500% to 1,200%) oversized and severely out of round. 
It is not uncommon to see the stem chest seat and bushings to be oversized and distorted 
on a unit in service. To fix the issue, the stem bushing bore is minimally resized to be 
round. The seat bore is then skim cut to be round while holding 0.004” concentricity to the 
stem bushing bore. This could have been completed in the NIDCO facility. However, this 
requires oversized stem bushing and seat parts which were not available. 
The bushings and seats were assembled as best possible. When the seats were installed, 
two (2) indicators were set up on the seat on an “X” and “Y” axis. The bolting was tightened 
until the gasket was just about to crush. The seat was then pushed to the extreme on each 
side of the “X” and “Y”, then pushed to the opposite side. The seat was then centered 
between the two values on both axes. The valves were then “slammed” shut as to self-align 
the valves to the seats. The bolting was then torqued per GE specification with indicators 
monitoring movement as the bolting was tightened. 
The V1 valve is the first line of defense in the event of an overspeed event. It is CRUCIAL 
that the valve discs align to the valve seats to have proper sealing. The unit can overspeed 
with only 3% of steam with no load on the generator. A catastrophic event is possible if the 
TTV were to fail and the V1 control valves did not seal. During the next outage it is 
recommended to machine the steam chest at the stem bushing and seat fits so that the fits 
are round and concentric to one another. Stem bushings and seats with stock should be 
ordered. The stem bushing with stock part number is PN# 101C459CA-101 (QTY5). The 
seat drawing does not have a part number that has extra stock. The original seat drawing is 
B709C06B. Five (5) new seats should be ordered and the manufacturer contacted to add 
0.125” at the “A” dimension (2 locations, upper and lower). If the manufacturer can not meet 
the request, an Engineering ER case should be opened for a weld procedure. The seats 
should be welded and machined down to 4.375” at the “A” dimension. The seats and welding 
(if needed) should be procured/fabricated well in advance of the outage.

Part Description: 
Flow to #5 steam extraction is controlled through a high-pressure oil hydraulically operated 
shell mounted axial flow grid type valve. Valve assembly consists of a multi-ported split ring 
that once rotated allows and controls steam flow through a respective, adjoining multi-ported 
split stationary diaphragm. Ring rotation is achieved through yoke- clevis-pivot block 
engagement, contrary to older versions that had a rack and gear configuration.
Valve cover and mounted actuator were disassembled from turbine’s upper half casing.
Upon turbine’s upper half shell disassembly and lift, grid valve was found in very good 
condition, able to slide easily by hand, without much effort. 
V2 valve; assembly and cover:
Valve’s upper and lower half rings and diaphragms were split and disassembled/ lifted from 
turbine to facilitate rotor’s removal. All four parts were shipped to NIDCO premises for 
aluminum oxide blasting and NDTs inspection and assessment.
Valve cover was sent later to NIDCO for machining, as new parts had been delivered 
oversized (upper guide, guide plate, front & rear guides) and had to be precision planned to 
design dimensions in order to obtain new rod alignment/ smooth slide and wear-free 
operation of the mechanism/ correct clearances at the slide/ proper and sealed reassembly. 
However, old guide plate reinstalled to keep the design dimensions.  Since planning were 
correctly executed as asked from NIDCO, guides’ underside added shims found during 
disassembly (had been installed in 2011 outage to compensate) were not re-installed.  
Valve’s rings and diaphragms were visually and MPI inspected after sand blasting, without 
findings. 
Bolting hardware (split joint) was replaced with new in the assembly and the valve cover 
(dowels, guide pins and screws).

-         All guides 
-         Valve’s rod and its spherical bearing/ snap ring, clevis, block-pivot and its pins,
-         Valve’s rod coupling (adapter), guide bushing, retainer flange and screws

The combined lubrication and control oil system was inspected during this outage. This 
included the disassembly, inspection and reassembly of the AC lube oil pumps, DC lube oil 
pump, vapor extractor and Lube Oil Coolers. Hydraulic pumps were replaced with new this 
outage.
DC lube oil pump was removed from the lube oil tank then disassembled and inspected. 
During ball bearing disassembly, a step was found on the pump shaft. Due to not having a 
replacement shaft onsite, ICL spare pump was used. Spare pump was disassembled and 
inspected. New ball bearings were installed. Dimensional checks were performed on the 
impeller, impeller casing and shaft. All dimensional checks were within tolerance and 
required no further action. Spare DC lube oil pump was reassembled without incident. Pump 
was installed in the lube oil tank with new gaskets.
AC lube oil pumps were removed from the lube oil tank, then disassembled and inspected. 
Pump motors were removed and given to ICL for shipment to third party vendor for 
refurbishment. No significant or unusual problems were noted during lube oil pump 
disassembly. Dimensional checks were performed on the impeller, impeller casing and shaft. 
All dimensional checks were within tolerance and required no further action. During this 
overhaul, ball bearings and oil seals were supplied by ICL and replaced. Associated 
discharge check valves were removed and visually inspected. Inspections revealed no 
deficiencies and were reinstalled with new gaskets. Both AC lube oil pumps have discharge 
butterfly valves. Vales were found with damaged rubber sealing surfaces. New butterfly 
valves were obtained from ICL and reinstalled. 
Hydraulic pumps were removed from the lube oil tank then sent to the ICL shop for storage. 
Hydraulic pump motors were given to ICL for shipment to third party vendor for 
refurbishment. ICL supplied new hydraulic pumps. One pump was brand new and the 
second was refurbished from a previous outage. Visual inspections were performed on the 
new pumps, and no deficiencies were noted. Pumps were checked to ensure that they were 
filled with oil prior to installation. Motors arrived back on site and were reinstalled on the lube 
oil tank without incident. New couplings were supplied by ICL and installed on hydraulic 
pumps and motors.
Accumulators underwent inspection and pre-charge was checked. Pre-charge was found to 
be less than 55.2 +/- 1.7 Bar per GEK 104154. Nitrogen accumulators were recharged and 
were found to be holding pressure at 54 Bar.

piping were removed and the lube oil coolers were inspected. Visual inspection revealed no 
deficiencies. Customer elected to remove cooler covers and water piping to perform a leak

This generator can come back to operation. 
It recommends to check periodically the cleaning on the inner casing floor and if there is oil try to understand 
where it come from and refurbish as soon as possible. The inspection can be done removing the air filter and 
see the floor between the bearing support and the inner shield. 
It recommends to follow the GEK 103566 for the next suggested outage.

General Electric performed on this generator a major outage as suggested by GEK103566 adding the field 
extraction after the Magic inspection performed in 2017 where it was find a large area of loose wedges.  
This generator has worked between 1-1-2015 to 29-11-2019 for 41130 hour, around 8300 hours/year close to a 
load of 20 MW .

 Complete re-wedge

 Turbine coupling
